query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: If a short-time, high-energy surface treatment is applied to CoCrFeMnNi-based high-entropy alloys, it will induce a stable, nanostructured tribofilm that promotes the in-situ formation and regeneration of lubricious oxides or compounds under friction, reducing both the coefficient of friction and wear rate from room temperature up to at least 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: Untreated CoCrFeMnNi-based high-entropy alloy with standard as-fabricated microstructure.
generation.intervention: A short, high-energy surface treatment (e.g., laser shock peening or friction-stir-based process) that refines near-surface grains and partially amorphizes the material, generating a robust surface tribofilm.
generation.conditions: Sliding contact under loads typical for mechanical moving parts at temperatures ranging from 25 °C to ~800 °C in air.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanograin boundaries and partially amorphized zones within the near-surface region that facilitate stable, self-replenishing tribofilms during high-temperature sliding.
generation.mechanism: Frictional heating activates tribochemical reactions in the refined near-surface layers, yielding a durable oxide or compound film that lowers local shear stresses and minimizes adhesive wear across a broad temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coefficient of friction and wear rate are reduced by at least 30% relative to untreated alloys over the 25–800 °C range.
generation.baseline: An untreated CoCrFeMnNi-based high-entropy alloy whose coarse microstructure does not reliably form or maintain a low-friction oxide layer under sliding.
generation.boundary: Beyond the treatment’s designed temperature or load thresholds, or under vacuum conditions without sufficient oxidative release, the tribofilm may degrade and no longer provide friction or wear benefits.
generation.uncertainty: Long-term durability of the tribofilm across repeated thermal cycles and extended sliding distances remains to be fully validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform pin-on-disk tests on treated and untreated alloy samples at five temperatures (25, 200, 400, 600, and 800 °C) under similar loads and sliding speeds to track changes in friction coefficients and wear rates over time.
measurements: Coefficient of friction over a fixed sliding distance at each temperature
Specific wear rate from measured mass or volume loss
Characterization of wear tracks and oxide films via SEM and EDS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, under any of the test conditions, the treated alloy exhibits friction or wear performance worse than or not significantly different from the untreated alloy, the hypothesis is falsified.

decision.trend: Earlier tribological studies on high-entropy alloys explored how ultra-fine or amorphized surface layers reduce friction and wear (PMC7311485). Researchers then investigated local reinforcements (e.g., laser-cladded WC-HEA) for improved wear resistance under demanding conditions (PMC8949536). More recent work highlights that nanohierarchical architectures with compositional undulation can sustain ultralow wear from ambient to high temperatures (PMC10241162). Additionally, 2D high-entropy alloy coatings have demonstrated self-lubricating tribo-catalytic properties under severe contact loads (PMC12019924). Despite these strides, a single, robust modification that ensures simultaneous friction and wear reduction under varying thermal conditions remains to be fully optimized.
decision.unsolved: While diverse approaches have lowered friction and wear in high-entropy alloys, a unifying treatment that adapts in situ and sustains lubrication across a broad temperature spectrum (from room temperature to several hundred °C) is still needed. The challenge is to maintain a protective interface film or surface structure that neither degrades nor delaminates under wide thermal and mechanical load variations.
decision.lever: Implement a short-time, high-energy surface treatment (e.g., controlled laser shock or friction-based process) that locally induces a stable, nanostructured tribofilm across the load-bearing regions. The treatment is tuned to develop a fine-grained or partially amorphized surface zone, which can form and regenerate lubricious oxide or compound layers during sliding.
decision.why: This intervention builds on reported benefits of near-surface nanostructuring (PMC7311485) and leverages in situ tribolayer formation (PMC10241162, PMC12019924). By generating a robust, self-replenishing boundary film, friction and wear can be reduced under varying thermal loads. The hypothesis is that the induced tribofilm, stabilized by nanograin boundaries and controlled oxidation, will maintain lubrication from ambient up to elevated temperatures. Previous studies suggest that dynamic transformations at the sliding interface can support low friction and wear; thus, combining an engineered near-surface microstructure with regulated thermal exposure may ensure stable self-lubrication. To falsify this hypothesis, a controlled sliding test over a broad temperature range (25–800 °C) could be conducted. If the friction coefficient and wear rate fail to remain consistently low (e.g., both escalate beyond those of the untreated alloy), the hypothesis would be invalidated.
